statement: Points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie on a circle in that order. Chords $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $P$. If $\angle ABD = 35^\circ$ and $\angle BDC = 40^\circ$, what is the degree measure of $\angle APB$?

choices.misconception: I used the half-difference rule for two secants from an outside point, (80 - 70)/2 = 5, but P is inside the circle.
I averaged the two given angles, (35 + 40)/2, as if angle APB were half the sum of the inscribed angles instead of half the sum of the arcs.
I used the arc BC = 80 degrees as angle BAC in triangle APB instead of half of it, so I got 180 - 35 - 80 = 65.
I found the angle between the chords on the other side, angle APD = (70 + 80)/2 = 75, which is supplementary to angle APB.

hints: Look at triangle $APB$. Which of its angles can you find?
Inscribed angles that stand on the same arc are equal. Angle $BAC$ stands on the same arc as angle $BDC$. Then use the angle sum in triangle $APB$.
$\angle BAP = \angle BAC = \angle BDC = 40^\circ$ and $\angle ABP = \angle ABD = 35^\circ$. The third angle of triangle $APB$ is what is left of $180^\circ$.

solutions.reliable: Angles $BAC$ and $BDC$ are inscribed angles on the same arc $BC$, so $\angle BAC = 40^\circ$. Since $P$ lies on $AC$ and on $BD$, triangle $APB$ has $\angle PAB = 40^\circ$ and $\angle PBA = 35^\circ$, so $\angle APB = 180^\circ - 40^\circ - 35^\circ = 105^\circ$. Check with arcs: arc $AD = 70^\circ$ and arc $BC = 80^\circ$, so arcs $AB + CD = 210^\circ$, and the angle between two chords is half the sum of the intercepted arcs, $210/2 = 105$. The transferable idea: in a circle, swap an angle you cannot see for an equal inscribed angle on the same arc.
solutions.elegant: The angle between two chords is half the sum of the arcs it and its vertical angle cut off. $\angle APD$ cuts off arcs $AD = 70^\circ$ and $BC = 80^\circ$, so $\angle APD = 75^\circ$ and $\angle APB = 180^\circ - 75^\circ = 105^\circ$.
